    <td
      class="d-block color-fg-default comment-body markdown-body js-comment-body"
      
    >
        <p dir="auto">As announced today in our <a href="https://developers.googleblog.com/an-important-update-transitioning-gemini-cli-to-antigravity-cli" rel="nofollow">full blog post</a>, we are unifying our agent-first development tools to better support complex, multi-agent workflows that many of you now run. To deliver the single platform you need to build the future, we are transitioning our terminal experience from Gemini CLI to the brand-new Antigravity CLI.</p>
<p dir="auto">Below I’ll summarize what this means for users of Gemini CLI:</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>🌟 Key changes &amp; Timeline</strong></p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><strong>Antigravity CLI is available today:</strong> Built in Go, the new CLI is snappier, supports asynchronous background workflows for complex tasks, and shares a unified architecture with the new Antigravity 2.0 desktop app. It retains our most critical features, including Agent Skills, Hooks, Subagents, and Extensions (now Antigravity plugins).</li>
<li><strong>Changes to Google AI Pro, Ultra, and free tier:</strong> On June 18, 2026, Gemini CLI will stop serving requests for Google AI Pro and Ultra, as well as those using it free of charge. These tiers are now supported via Antigravity CLI. This change also applies to those using Gemini CLI via Gemini Code Assist IDE extensions and Gemini Code Assist on GitHub.</li>
<li><strong>Enterprise access remains unchanged:</strong> If your organization uses Gemini CLI or our IDE extensions via a Gemini Code Assist Standard or Enterprise license, or through Google Cloud, your access remains fully supported. Gemini CLI will also remain accessible via paid Gemini and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform API keys. If you want to try Antigravity CLI, you can use it now with your Google Cloud projects.</li>
<li><strong>Open Source:</strong> You will continue to see us work on GitHub as we keep Gemini CLI updated with latest model releases, bugs and security fixes for our enterprise customers. The project remains available to the community as an Apache 2.0 licensed repository with no changes.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">We understand this transition will require some planning. We are here to help make the move to Antigravity CLI and Antigravity 2.0 as smooth as possible, we have put together a <a href="http://antigravity.google/docs/gcli-migration" rel="nofollow">migration guide</a> that includes an FAQ, and we will be releasing video walkthroughs in the coming weeks.</p>
<p dir="auto">Thank you folks,</p>
<p dir="auto">Dmitry Lyalin</p>
    </td>
  </tr>

        <tr class="d-block">
    <td
      class="d-block color-fg-default comment-body markdown-body js-comment-body tmp-px-3 pt-0 pb-2"
      
    >
        <p dir="auto">Hello Gemini team! Thank you for the impressive work on transitioning to the Antigravity CLI. The performance improvements and the new agentic architecture are fantastic.</p>
<p dir="auto">Previously, when using gemini-cli, I heavily relied on authenticating via my Google AI Studio API key to access the Gemma 4 model. This combination was the cornerstone of my daily local development workflow for quick, lightweight, and efficient tasks.</p>
<ol dir="auto">
<li>
<p dir="auto">The Problem<br>
With the upgrade to Antigravity CLI, the ability to log in using a standard Google AI Studio API key seems to have been removed or heavily restricted. This change effectively locks out independent developers like myself from accessing Gemma 4 in the terminal, completely breaking the local tooling environment we have come to rely on.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto">Why This Matters<br>
Google's core vision for the Gemma family has always been to make state-of-the-art AI accessible to a broad audience of developers, researchers, and hobbyists. By restricting API access in the new CLI:</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Community Friction: Individual developers, students, and open-source contributors who rely on the accessible tiers of Google AI Studio are left behind.</p>
<p dir="auto">Slower Model Adoption: Reducing the friction to use Gemma 4 directly in the terminal is the best way to encourage developers to build with, test, and advocate for Google's models.</p>
<ol start="3" dir="auto">
<li>Proposed Solution<br>
To better serve the broader community, I would like to request the following additions to Antigravity CLI:</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Re-introduce AI Studio API Login: Provide an explicit pathway (e.g., an agy login --api-key command or reading the GEMINI_API_KEY environment variable) for users to authenticate via Google AI Studio without requiring a full enterprise or Google Cloud setup.</p>
<p dir="auto">Add Gemma 4 to the Model Roster: Ensure that Gemma 4 is explicitly available and selectable in the model list for users authenticated this way.</p>
<p dir="auto">Thank you for your time and for considering the needs of the broader developer community. We would love to continue using Antigravity CLI as our primary daily driver!</p>
    </td>
  </tr>

    </tbody>
  </table>
</task-lists>

    <tbody

    >
        <tr class="d-block">
    <td
      class="d-block color-fg-default comment-body markdown-body js-comment-body"
      
    >
        <p dir="auto">Having tried Antigravity CLI, my first impressions are that it seems to be a buggy, token-burning mess. Gemini CLI by no means was perfect, but you had per-model quotas that, although reduced from what they were when I first got my subscription, were reasonable enough to be useable throughout the day. Not to mention more control. Antigravity just goes ahead and makes changes to files. Gemini CLI was good in that you could read the changes and if it was botching something, stop it and correct it. Now you need source control like Git with frequent commits (before completely implementing the feature), to ensure that it doesn't botch good code.</p>
<p dir="auto">Antigravity's token burning combined with strict limits (shared across all Gemini models), has meant that what previously could have been 5-8 hours of work before exhausting my quotas is now burned in 10-20 minutes. Additionally, no option to compress chat history, etc. Many of the useful features that gave Gemini CLI polish are missing. Even if they are added, the transition to a closed source model is a massive rug-pull and the lack of quality and refinement that was present in this project is clear. Bragging about how many stars you got on GitHub while closed-sourcing the project is pretty tone-deaf. Bad move Google.</p>
<p dir="auto">I will be cancelling my subscription as soon as the year is up and moving to Claude or Codex unless Google backpedals on this.</p>
<p dir="auto">Gemini CLI was great, despite some of its shortfalls. It's a shame that it's effectively being discontinued.</p>
    </td>
  </tr>

    </tbody>
  </table>
</task-lists>

    <td
      class="d-block color-fg-default comment-body markdown-body js-comment-body"
      
    >
        <p dir="auto">Hello everyone, sad day for Gemini CLI, but I believe Antigravity CLI will be fixed and better soon.</p>
<p dir="auto">As Antigravity usage may continue to grow, I built a new package called <strong><a href="https://github.com/HoangP8/tokless">tokless</a></strong> with a simple philosophy: <em>saving tokens shouldn't be complicated. While there are many great plugins out there to help coding agents save context and improve performance, setting them up and keeping them updated is often too complex—especially for non-technical users.</em></p>
<h3 dir="auto"><code class="notranslate">tokless</code>: The Ultimate "Lazy" Solution</h3>
<p dir="auto">Run a single command, select <strong>Antigravity</strong>, and your entire environment (both IDE and CLI) is instantly configured.<br>
<a target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" href="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/120444105/610199482-b8b82446-cad7-49cb-8a7e-3808cac654b0.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3ODg3NTY0ODMsIm5iZiI6MTc4ODc1NjE4MywicGF0aCI6Ii8xMjA0NDQxMDUvNjEwMTk5NDgyLWI4YjgyNDQ2LWNhZDctNDljYi04YTdlLTM4MDhjYWM2NTRiMC5wbmc_.STQfIoZHih48W4nhCtR0JO2BZYLgJyVeghS2WE3SjGo"><img width="1585" height="732" alt="Screenshot 2026-06-18 232932" src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/120444105/610199482-b8b82446-cad7-49cb-8a7e-3808cac654b0.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3ODg3NTY0ODMsIm5iZiI6MTc4ODc1NjE4MywicGF0aCI6Ii8xMjA0NDQxMDUvNjEwMTk5NDgyLWI4YjgyNDQ2LWNhZDctNDljYi04YTdlLTM4MDhjYWM2NTRiMC5wbmc_.STQfIoZHih48W4nhCtR0JO2BZYLgJyVeghS2WE3SjGo" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto; max-height: 732px;; aspect-ratio: 1585 / 732; background-color: var(--bgColor-muted); border-radius: 6px" class="js-gh-image-fallback"></a></p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Just one <code class="notranslate">curl</code> line: Choose Antigravity, and it's completely ready to go.</li>
<li>Zero extra configuration: No need to configure anything manually.</li>
<li>Just restart your agent to start saving tokens and your context window.</li>
<li>Fully open-source &amp; minimal setup!</li>
</ul>
<h3 dir="auto">What's Included?</h3>
<p dir="auto">This package automatically enables 4 tools:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><strong>CodeGraph</strong> (Code Discovery)</li>
<li><strong>RTK</strong> (Terminal Output Filtering)</li>
<li><strong>Context-Mode</strong> (Task Execution Sandbox)</li>
<li><strong>Caveman</strong> (Minimal Agent Responses)</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<p dir="auto">If you encounter any issues or compatibility problems with your specific setup, please don't hesitate to raise an issue on the repo.<br>
If you find this tool useful, I would really appreciate a star!</p>

        <div class="edit-comment-hide">

        <tr class="d-block">
    <td
      class="d-block color-fg-default comment-body markdown-body js-comment-body"
      
    >
        <p dir="auto">This is bullshit. Let's call it what it is, highway robbery.</p>
<p dir="auto">They realized people could use Gemini CLI effectively for hours, get real work done, and actually be productive. So they put a stop to it.</p>
<p dir="auto">Not only that, they shipped a substandard, half baked Go binary that's packed with bizarre junk. Don't believe me? Run <code class="notranslate">strings</code> on it yourself.</p>
<p dir="auto">Instead of a lean coding assistant, you'll find references to browser automation, Chrome DevTools, Playwright, persistent conversation history, context windows, long term memory, knowledge bases, telemetry, analytics, experimentation frameworks, feature flags, browser subagents, remote workspaces, indexing services, trajectory tracking, console log collection, feedback collection, and enough internal Google infrastructure to make you wonder whether you're looking at a coding assistant or someone's monorepo accidentally compiled into a single executable.</p>
<p dir="auto">And then there are the little gems that somehow survived the trip into production. My personal favorite has to be:</p>
<p dir="auto"><code class="notranslate">/Users/gableroux/somewhere/.vagrant/machines/default/virtualbox/private_key</code></p>
<p dir="auto">No, I don't think Google accidentally shipped somebody's private key. But I do appreciate the archaeological artifact from someone's development environment. It's like opening the hood of a brand new Ferrari and finding the mechanic's lunch still sitting on the engine. It's the kind of thing that makes you wonder what they actually cleaned up before release.</p>
<p dir="auto">The binary is also littered with references to internal projects like Antigravity, Cortex, Jetbox, Mendel, Cascade, KnowledgeBaseService, trajectory management, browser agents, persistent memory, and countless debugging and telemetry components. Maybe every single one of those has a perfectly innocent explanation. Maybe they don't. Either way, this is an astonishing amount of baggage for what's supposed to be a command line coding assistant.</p>
<p dir="auto">Then there's the user experience. It doesn't matter whether you're on the Free tier or the Pro tier. The CLI happily burns through your context window with long winded monologues, unnecessary tool invocations, random detours, and excessive reasoning that completely ignores what you actually asked. Every wasted token is quota or money you paid for.</p>
<p dir="auto">And before anyone says, "That's just how modern software works," spare me. Most users aren't paying for every unnecessary paragraph their AI decides to write. Every pointless tangent costs tokens. Every token costs money or eats into your quota. If your business model depends on making the model talk twice as much to accomplish half as much, don't be surprised when people start asking uncomfortable questions.</p>
<p dir="auto">Don't trust me. Run <code class="notranslate">strings $(which agy)</code> yourself. Spend ten minutes reading through it. At the very least, you'll start asking why a supposedly lightweight coding assistant contains references to browser automation, persistent memory systems, telemetry pipelines, experimentation platforms, conversation history, knowledge bases, analytics, and what looks like half of Google's internal ecosystem. Running <code class="notranslate">strings</code> on this thing feels less like reverse engineering and more like rummaging through someone's desk after they forgot to clean up before shipping. At some point you stop asking, "Why is this here?" and start asking, "What exactly did they remove before release?"<br>
Yeah... Enjoy Google's Antigravity where both the users and the agents are test subjects and humans made to pay for the privilege.</p>
    </td>
  </tr>

    </tbody>
  </table>
</task-lists>

<p dir="auto">Hey 👋 I'm <code class="notranslate">gableroux</code>, most likely the one from that <code class="notranslate">/Users/gableroux/somewhere/.vagrant/machines/default/virtualbox/private_key</code> and I dug into this a bit.</p>

<span class="pl-c"><span class="pl-c">#</span> 3. the private key block</span>
strings <span class="pl-s"><span class="pl-pds">$(</span>which agy<span class="pl-pds">)</span></span> <span class="pl-k">|</span> grep -A27 -i <span class="pl-s"><span class="pl-pds">'</span>begin private key<span class="pl-pds">'</span></span></pre></div>
<p dir="auto">A few things:</p>
<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="1. I haven't touched `vagrant` in ages 😂

2. `/Users/gableroux/somewhere/.vagrant/machines/default/virtualbox/private_key` doesn't exist on my system (for what it's worth). Looks like an example/placeholder path from a vendored lib that just happens to be baked into the binary, and there are other placeholder home dirs like `/Users/johnsmith/` and `/Users/hubery/` sitting right next to it. 🤷

3. The private key you can pull out (public fingerprint: `SHA256:S48lELVdqzwUyaYeRTduLGcPU70yHh3CFsu0rN+L3/E`) returns no match online (from what I could find) and no hit against any of my personal keys. It's a valid RSA-2048 key, but it gives access to nothing of mine. You won't be stealing my GitHub account with it. 🍭

4. I really don't think that private key is related to the `.vagrant/.../private_key` path at all. Different part of the binary, different feature. They just both happened to show up in `strings`."><pre class="notranslate"><code class="notranslate">1. I haven't touched `vagrant` in ages 😂

2. `/Users/gableroux/somewhere/.vagrant/machines/default/virtualbox/private_key` doesn't exist on my system (for what it's worth). Looks like an example/placeholder path from a vendored lib that just happens to be baked into the binary, and there are other placeholder home dirs like `/Users/johnsmith/` and `/Users/hubery/` sitting right next to it. 🤷

3. The private key you can pull out (public fingerprint: `SHA256:S48lELVdqzwUyaYeRTduLGcPU70yHh3CFsu0rN+L3/E`) returns no match online (from what I could find) and no hit against any of my personal keys. It's a valid RSA-2048 key, but it gives access to nothing of mine. You won't be stealing my GitHub account with it. 🍭

4. I really don't think that private key is related to the `.vagrant/.../private_key` path at all. Different part of the binary, different feature. They just both happened to show up in `strings`.
</code></pre></div>
<p dir="auto">So, plenty of other stuff in that binary too, sure, but I guess my username is now just a popular example macOS home directory path.</p>
<p dir="auto">Don't leak your keys, stay safe and don't believe everything without verifying yourself. 🙏</p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<p dir="auto">Gabe, it's a genuine honor to meet one of the original developers of the Gemini CLI. I absolutely loved that little baby. Sure, it had its quirks, but compared to the absolute monstrosity that is Antigravity, the old CLI looks like a saint. Please don't take this personally. It's just a well deserved critique of what essentially feels like getting mugged in a digital alleyway by Google.</p>
<p dir="auto">When a tool torches months of a budget in a few hours and achieves absolutely nothing, the line between a technical oversight and an intentional heist gets pretty blurry. The result is exactly the same. The user's wallet is empty, and the platform is laughing all the way to the bank. I'd avoid calling it a legal scam, just kidding, I totally call it that. It's a legal scam designed to milk users dry, built on economic incentives that literally reward gross incompetence. If a regular app hogs memory and crashes costing users money, users riot, and the company tanks. When Google ships an AI agent that hogs context, they just start printing money because every single extra token is billable.</p>
<p dir="auto">To rub some salt in the wound, users are basically paying Google to generate their telemetry data. After tearing apart the binary, I found a massive sprawling city of infrastructure for Battle Mode evaluation, trajectory recording, experiment management, and state caching. What I didn't find was a shred of client side cost control. So small developers like us are effectively subsidizing Google's inference costs while building their next training dataset for free. The perfect business model. We , the muppets and the Gemini models are both test subjects :).</p>
<p dir="auto">Since you've dug through the binary yourself, you know exactly how much junk is baked into the binary. There's a hilarious disconnect between the cute, simple CLI we see and the terrifying multi agent hydra lurking underneath. If anyone is using pay as you go billing, this thing turns into an absolute token incinerator.</p>
<p dir="auto">Aside from reading the same files over and over, the biggest fuel for this token bonfire seems to be the orchestration and telemetry setup. My analysis dug up symbols like experiments.MendelStateCache, RecordCortexTrajectory, RecordCortexTrajectoryStep, GetRedactionInfo, redactCortexTrajectory, BattleModeMetadata, GetParentCascadeId, JetboxSubscribeToSummariesRequest, FEATURE_USAGE_TYPE_CASCADE_BROWSER, and agent_response_negative_feedback_submitted. Together they indicate a massive obsession with experiment management, usage tracking, and multi agent juggling and an absulte disregard for the paying users.</p>
<p dir="auto">It also looks like the runtime doesn't even know the meaning of context pruning. During diagnostic loops, subagents just keep swallowing huge parent contexts, gorging on entire command outputs, source files, and headers. My forensic deep dive caught individual requests casually swallowing over a million input tokens. I watched a runaway session chew through roughly 600 million tokens, torching 70 quid in API credits just to solve a problem that was already fixed.</p>
<p dir="auto">The scariest part is the complete absence of any meaningful client side cost awareness. There are no token budgets, no spending limits, and no emergency brakes to stop a developer from accidentally funding a small nation. Usually, users only realize they've been financially ruined when they finally check their cloud billing dashboard.</p>
<p dir="auto">It was definitely a fun easter egg finding references to your old development environment in there, but the architecture itself is the real nightmare. Based on what I saw, Google heavily prioritizes aggressive telemetry and multi agent orchestration while completely forgetting to protect developers from catastrophic, wallet draining token consumption.</p>
<p dir="auto">Greeting from the sunny climes of London UK bud.</p>
<p dir="auto">Gorilla</p>

        <div class="email-fragment">To whom this may concern,

I am writing to share some observations regarding the recent transition
from the Gemini CLI to the Antigravity CLI and the broader shifts occurring
within the ecosystem.

It has become increasingly clear that these changes represent more than
just a standard product migration; the Gemini framework is being
fundamentally restructured, leaving the legacy CLI as collateral damage. We
are witnessing a significant transformation where traditional programming
is rapidly being replaced by a model of digital stewardship. This shift is
unfolding incrementally—line by line and precept by precept—leading toward
a reality that few in the industry fully anticipated.

The current state of the tooling suggests that the industry is essentially
consuming its previous foundations to build something entirely different.
It is concerning that these shifts are occurring without a more transparent
acknowledgement of the impact on individual developers and the fundamental
nature of our work.

I believe it is vital to recognize these developments for what they are as
we navigate this new landscape.

Best regards,

Russell Nordland</div>

      <div class="color-bg-default border-bottom position-relative">
        <div class="edit-comment-hide">

    >
        <tr class="d-block">
    <td
      class="d-block color-fg-default comment-body markdown-body js-comment-body"
      
    >
        <p dir="auto">I was wondering if anything has changed since my last <a class="issue-link js-issue-link" data-error-text="Failed to load title" data-id="10095218" data-permission-text="Title is private" data-url="https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/discussions/27274" data-hovercard-type="discussion" data-hovercard-url="/google-gemini/gemini-cli/discussions/27274/hovercard?comment_id=17015927" href="https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/discussions/27274#discussioncomment-17015927">#27274 (comment)</a> asking about the privacy changes in Antigravity, so I run a deep search on this.</p>
<p dir="auto">It seems nothing changed. I just thought maybe all this was some misunderstanding or Google just forgot to clarify something in terms of use, but all facts suggest that this was a deliberate change by Google.</p>
<p dir="auto">If anyone is interested, see the below.</p>
<details>
<summary>🤖 <b>Short version:</b> nothing fundamental has changed yet. For consumer Antigravity, Google still treats your prompts/code as “Interactions” that can be stored, reviewed by humans, and used to improve models unless you’re under Workspace/GCP/Enterprise terms or explicitly opt out where that’s possible—and even there, the opt‑out mechanisms are still partially ambiguous and coupled to other features like history.</summary>
<h2 dir="auto">Antigravity consumer vs Workspace/GCP</h2>
<h3 dir="auto">Additional Terms still say “we use your Interactions”</h3>
<p dir="auto">The Antigravity Additional Terms of Service are unchanged in spirit since your comment: they explicitly say that when you use Antigravity, Google records and stores your “user data, interaction data, related metadata and any feedback” and uses these “Interactions” to evaluate, develop and improve Google/Alphabet products and machine learning technologies, with employees and contractors able to access and review them. <a href="https://jorgep.com/blog/google-antigravity-additional-terms-of-service/" rel="nofollow">jorgep</a></p>
<p dir="auto">There is a settings‑based opt‑out line in those terms:</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">“If you don’t want your Interactions used in this way, navigate to settings to change your preference on how such data is used.” <a href="https://jorgep.com/blog/google-antigravity-additional-terms-of-service/" rel="nofollow">jorgep</a></p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">But this is not mirrored by a clearly labeled “don’t use my prompts/code for training” toggle in the UI—only the <strong>Enable Telemetry</strong> switch, which is what triggered the ambiguity you called out. Forum threads show people are still confused and pressing Google on this exact gap as of Feb–Jun 2026. <a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/urgent-data-deletion-opt-out-request-ignored-missing-privacy-settings/121602" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a></p>
<h3 dir="auto">Newer carve‑out: Workspace/GCP sessions</h3>
<p dir="auto">One important nuance that <em>has</em> become clearer since your original comment: Google’s own wording now explicitly distinguishes Workspace/GCP access from pure consumer use.</p>
<p dir="auto">In a developer forum thread, a user quotes updated Antigravity language:</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">“Notwithstanding the foregoing, if you are accessing the Service via Google Workspace or the Google Cloud Platform, <strong>we will not collect your prompts, content, or model responses.</strong>” <a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/antigravity-data-training-opt-out/125236" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a></p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">That matches the positioning in the official “Google Antigravity for enterprises” blog: if you connect Antigravity via GCP, you’re going through the <strong>Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform</strong>, which inherits standard Google Cloud data governance. They state that “enterprise prompts, responses, code, or other such telemetry is not stored outside of your private environments,” and that billing is consumption‑based at Agent Platform pricing rather than via Google AI subscriptions. <a href="https://www.inteeka.com/insights/google-antigravity-gemini-spark-enterprise-agents" rel="nofollow">inteeka</a></p>
<p dir="auto">Practically:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Consumer login (“Continue with Google”)</strong><br>
Your data falls under consumer Antigravity terms: prompts/code are stored as Interactions and can be used for training and human review, unless the Telemetry/interaction setting truly disables that (see below). <a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/antigravity-data-training-opt-out/125236" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a></p>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Workspace / GCP login</strong><br>
If Antigravity is tied to a Workspace org or GCP project, the carve‑out says prompts/content/model responses are <em>not</em> collected for those enterprise sessions, and data governance follows Cloud’s CDPA (no training on customer data, private boundary). <a href="https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern" rel="nofollow">docs.cloud.google</a></p>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This is the closest thing to a clear statement that you can avoid training <em>without</em> “pay per token” in the narrow sense of Cloud API use—<em>if</em> your org is on Workspace/GCP and Antigravity is correctly bound to that identity. But for most individual devs, the only way to get those protections is indeed Cloud/Enterprise, which is consumption‑billed. <a href="https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/genai_privacy_google_cloud.pdf" rel="nofollow">services.google</a></p>
<h2 dir="auto">“Enable Telemetry” and whether it actually stops training</h2>
<h3 dir="auto">What Google says officially</h3>
<p dir="auto">Google’s documentation and support replies treat <strong>Enable Telemetry</strong> as the primary data‑collection switch for Antigravity:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Docs and TOS copies say that when Telemetry is <strong>on</strong>, Antigravity “collects interactions for use in evaluating, developing, and improving Antigravity and models that support Antigravity.” <a href="https://note.com/shimer_system/n/n0c0772a9359b" rel="nofollow">note</a></li>
<li>A support reply in the “urgent data deletion / opt‑out missing” thread describes Telemetry as “the primary mechanism for managing usage data collection” and claims that disabling it “stops the collection of interactions data and diagnostic information used to improve the service.” <a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/urgent-data-deletion-opt-out-request-ignored-missing-privacy-settings/121602" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a></li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Several Japanese/English walkthroughs for Antigravity’s privacy settings interpret it the same way: Telemetry on → interactions are collected and used to improve Antigravity and underlying models; Telemetry off → “data collection is off” for Antigravity, at least as far as those interactions. <a href="https://note.com/tyaperujp01/n/n0b0a209feda6" rel="nofollow">note</a></p>
<h3 dir="auto">What remains ambiguous</h3>
<p dir="auto">However, this is <em>still</em> not spelled out in the Additional Terms as “if Telemetry is off, we will not use your prompts/code for training.” The terms only positively describe what happens when Telemetry is <strong>on</strong>, and forum users keep pointing out that this is legally different from a clear negative guarantee. <a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/how-can-i-completely-opt-out-of-the-use-of-my-data-for-model-training/168429" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a></p>
<p dir="auto">You can see this tension in the dev forum threads you cross‑linked:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Multiple users note that the only available toggle is “Enable Telemetry,” and it is “technically distinct from ‘Interaction Data’ used for AI model training.” <a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/how-can-i-completely-opt-out-of-the-use-of-my-data-for-model-training/168429" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a></li>
<li>Others insist that Google staff previously said disabling Telemetry means opting out of data training—but they can’t find authoritative written confirmation in current docs/TOS and call that out as confusing or inconsistent. <a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/antigravity-privacy/138277" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a></li>
<li>A more recent reply says flatly: “disabling telemetry won’t stop Google from training on your repo/codebase and your prompts. Telemetry is a different thing than not using your data for training their AI models.” That’s not an official statement, but it reflects how privacy‑sensitive users are still reading the situation. <a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/antigravity-privacy/138277" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a></li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Net: Google has nudged documentation to imply Telemetry controls training, but they have <em>not</em> explicitly resolved the ambiguity in the legal text. If you need strong guarantees, you still have to assume consumer Antigravity sessions are training‑eligible unless you are under Workspace/GCP/Enterprise terms.</p>
<h2 dir="auto">Billing vs privacy: “still capture everything unless you pay per token?”</h2>
<p dir="auto">For Antigravity itself, the situation is basically what you described, with more explicit wording now:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Consumer Antigravity (Pro/Ultra, free)</strong></p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Runs under Antigravity Additional Terms + consumer Gemini terms. Interactions are recorded, stored, and used to improve Google services and ML. <a href="https://jorgep.com/blog/google-antigravity-additional-terms-of-service/" rel="nofollow">jorgep</a></li>
<li>Telemetry off <em>probably</em> reduces or stops this collection, but the guarantee is not crystal‑clear in the TOS. <a href="https://note.com/shimer_system/n/n0c0772a9359b" rel="nofollow">note</a></li>
<li>There is no dedicated “do not use my prompts/code for model training” toggle independent of Telemetry. <a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/urgent-data-deletion-opt-out-request-ignored-missing-privacy-settings/121602" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a></li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Antigravity via Google Cloud project / Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform</strong></p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Governed by Google Cloud ToS + Cloud generative AI privacy addendum. Customer data (prompts, responses, code) is not used to train foundation models and is not stored outside your private environment. <a href="https://www.inteeka.com/insights/google-antigravity-gemini-spark-enterprise-agents" rel="nofollow">inteeka</a></li>
<li>There is still abuse‑monitoring in GCP generative AI: Cloud ToS explicitly allows Google to log prompts to review potential AUP violations. That logging is <em>for abuse detection</em>, not training. <a href="https://cloud.google.com/terms" rel="nofollow">cloud.google</a></li>
<li>Billing is consumption‑based at Agent Platform pricing, i.e., “per token” or per usage unit, not via flat subscriptions. <a href="https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/genai_privacy_google_cloud.pdf" rel="nofollow">services.google</a></li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">So your summary “Google ended subscriptions with no‑training protections; if you want strong privacy you must accept API‑key‑style consumption billing” is still essentially right for individual Antigravity users. There is now explicit legal language to protect Workspace/GCP usage in Antigravity, but it’s tied to enterprise identity and Cloud terms, not to consumer AI Pro/Ultra subscriptions. <a href="https://www.inteeka.com/insights/google-antigravity-gemini-spark-enterprise-agents" rel="nofollow">inteeka</a></p>
<h2 dir="auto">Gemini web (Apps) – status as of July 2026</h2>
<p dir="auto">On Gemini web (gemini.google.com), the privacy model is a bit more clearly documented, and hasn’t fundamentally changed from what you described:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><strong>Gemini Apps Privacy Hub</strong>, updated July 15, 2026, describes “Gemini Apps Activity”: by default, your prompts, outputs, and some associated metadata can be saved, reviewed by human raters, and used to improve models. [<a href="https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en" rel="nofollow">support.google</a>](<a href="https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en" rel="nofollow">https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en</a>)</li>
<li>If you <strong>turn off Gemini Apps Activity</strong>, Google’s own docs and multiple independent guides agree on two key points:
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Future conversations are not sent to human reviewers and not used to train Gemini’s generative ML models. <a href="https://www.tomsguide.com/ai/google-gemini/how-to-stop-gemini-from-training-on-your-data" rel="nofollow">tomsguide</a></li>
<li>However, even with Activity off, conversations are retained for up to 72 hours for service and safety; and any data previously selected for human review may be kept (de‑linked from your account) for up to three years. <a href="https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39426668" rel="nofollow">news.ycombinator</a></li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Critically:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Turning off Activity also disables history and some Workspace extensions—so privacy is coupled to UX and integration, exactly as you noted. <a href="https://support.google.com/gemini/thread/440410885/overwhelmed-by-gemini-data-collection-can-i-use-it-without-giving-up-privacy?hl=en" rel="nofollow">support.google</a></li>
<li>There is still no way to say “do not train on my data, but keep full history and personalization.” This coupling is now a documented pain point; users have opened feature requests to decouple training opt‑out from chat history visibility, but as of July 2026 it’s still tied together. <a href="https://support.google.com/gemini/thread/430133908/critical-feature-request-decouple-data-training-opt-out-from-chat-history-visibility?hl=ja" rel="nofollow">support.google</a></li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">For enterprises, there’s a separate track:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><strong>Gemini for Google Cloud / Gemini Enterprise</strong> makes the standard cloud promise: prompts/responses not used to train models by default, under CDPA. <a href="https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/generative-ai/generative-ai-in-google-workspace-privacy-hub" rel="nofollow">knowledge.workspace.google</a></li>
<li>Gemini Apps Community answers explicitly say: your options to prevent training are either (a) turn off Gemini Apps Activity (for consumer/Google One AI Premium), or (b) use Gemini for Google Cloud (Enterprise) where prompts/responses are not used for training by default. <a href="https://support.google.com/gemini/thread/386101670/gemini-subscription-tiers-that-restrict-data-usage-for-model-training?hl=en" rel="nofollow">support.google</a></li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Again, the pattern is: privacy and “no training” are a Cloud/Enterprise feature and an opt‑out setting; subscriptions alone do not guarantee that your data is untouched.</p>
<h2 dir="auto">Community sentiment and whether ambiguity is resolved</h2>
<p dir="auto">From the threads you linked and follow‑on discussions:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Developers and privacy‑conscious users are <em>still</em> complaining that Antigravity’s UI and TOS don’t give a clear, user‑visible guarantee that disabling Telemetry fully stops training on prompts and code. [<a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/urgent-data-deletion-opt-out-request-ignored-missing-privacy-settings/121602" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a>](<a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/how-can-i-completely-opt-out-of-the-use-of-my-data-for-model-training/168429" rel="nofollow">https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/how-can-i-completely-opt-out-of-the-use-of-my-data-for-model-training/168429</a>)</li>
<li>Some support replies claim Telemetry off is “opting out of use of my data for model training,” but that’s contradicted by other statements and not backed by precise legal language, so people are skeptical. <a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/antigravity-privacy/138277" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a></li>
<li>Several blogs, note.com articles, and YouTube walkthroughs exist solely to explain how to “minimize” or “prevent” data training in Antigravity and Gemini, which is a signal that the built‑in UX and documentation aren’t addressing developer trust. <a href="https://note.com/ritsuto2525/n/nea038b75697c?hl=en" rel="nofollow">note</a></li>
<li>Criticism like “this is a backdoor privacy and cost change masked as a product change” (from the GitHub discussion) is still echoed in more recent think‑pieces about “the Google trap” for devs using Antigravity/Gemini in their workflows. <a href="https://abumchisom.com/articles/the-google-trap-software-developers-founders-are-walking-right-in-and-never-know" rel="nofollow">abumchisom</a></li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">I didn’t find any credible indication of upcoming changes that would:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Separate “model training” from “activity/history” in Gemini Apps, or</li>
<li>Add an explicit, dedicated “no training on prompts/code” toggle to Antigravity that’s clearly spelled out in the Additional Terms.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The currently documented “fix” for sensitive/commercial data remains:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Use <strong>Workspace/GCP / Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform</strong>, where prompts/code aren’t used to train foundation models and stay in your Cloud boundary (with some abuse‑monitoring logging). <a href="https://cloud.google.com/terms" rel="nofollow">cloud.google</a></li>
<li>Or turn off <strong>Gemini Apps Activity</strong> for Gemini web, accepting the loss of history and some integrations, plus the limited 72‑hour retention. <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=koMBvLM-luc" rel="nofollow">youtube</a></li>
</ul>
<h2 dir="auto">How to reason about it for your own use</h2>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Consumer Antigravity (Pro/Ultra, “Continue with Google”)</strong><br>
Assume prompts/code are training‑eligible and may be human‑reviewed unless you see a written, explicit guarantee tying Telemetry‑off to “no training,” which does not currently exist in the TOS. Telemetry‑off likely <em>reduces</em> collection, but treat it as best‑effort analytics suppression, not a hard governance boundary. [<a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/antigravity-data-training-opt-out/125236" rel="nofollow">discuss.ai.google</a>](<a href="https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/urgent-data-deletion-opt-out-request-ignored-missing-privacy-settings/121602" rel="nofollow">https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/urgent-data-deletion-opt-out-request-ignored-missing-privacy-settings/121602</a>)</p>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Antigravity with GCP project / Workspace identity</strong><br>
You get Cloud’s CDPA protections: prompts/responses not used to train models, kept in your private environment, but with consumption‑based billing and abuse‑monitoring logging. This is the only clearly documented non‑training path that also leaves you with full functionality. <a href="https://cloud.google.com/terms" rel="nofollow">cloud.google</a></p>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Gemini web (Ultra/Advanced/Google One AI Premium)</strong><br>
If you want “no training,” you must turn off <strong>Gemini Apps Activity</strong>, and accept loss of history and the 72‑hour transient retention. There is no way to remain on Ultra with full history while completely blocking training. <a href="https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en" rel="nofollow">support.google</a></p>
</li>
</ul>
</details>
    </td>
  </tr>

        <blockquote>
<p dir="auto"><a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/ilya-id/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/ilya-id">@ilya-id</a> No. I did not want anything from you :) I was sharing findings, that is it. Anyway. If this changed – great. But still to re-iterate my main point is:</p>
<p dir="auto">Using data of personal accounts, paying money for subscriptions is still not ok and has never been.</p>
<p dir="auto">This is still shit one way or another. If a company wants to be clear and transparent about privacy, they are. It is not hard to implement a checkbox "I do not let to use my data for AI training". Google, on the other hand, makes you check "I let share my data" right when you log in into AG, even from the workspace account (I tried today out of curiosity), then pointing to terms saying that it may not apply to them. But what else should you expect from Google?</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">"If a company wants to be clear and transparent about privacy," I liked that one.</p>
<p dir="auto">Run a manual strings analysis on the Gemini CLI and agy, and you will see the extent they care about privacy. They worked really hard on it by embedding <code class="notranslate">ms-playwright-go/1.57.0</code>, making use of Mendel (<code class="notranslate">experiments.MendelStateCache</code>), <code class="notranslate">RecordCortexTrajectory</code>, and <code class="notranslate">RecordCortexTrajectoryStep</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto">And the best one, wait for it... When they send data back home they use redaction on the client (<code class="notranslate">redactCortexTrajectory</code>). It generates a <code class="notranslate">GetRedactionInfo</code> manifest that tells Google exactly what was stripped from the user payload. So it is like, we care so much for you and your privacy so much so that before the telemetry was sent we redacted it, all your personal data that could identify you has been stripped AND WE HAVE THE PROOF OF WHAT WAS REDACTED BECAUSE WE REDACTED IT :)</p>

      class="d-block color-fg-default comment-body markdown-body js-comment-body tmp-px-3 pt-0 pb-2"
      
    >
        <blockquote>
<p dir="auto">I had a project i was working on gemin cli, how do i export my chat history and etc to antigravity? This is so annoying. Everything was ok before these changes.</p>
</blockquote>
<h1 dir="auto">All chat history for gemini cli antigravity-cli is stored in ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">1. Export the SQLite database containing conversation summaries</h1>
<p dir="auto">sqlite3 ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/conversation_summaries.db .dump &gt; summaries.sql</p>
<h1 dir="auto">2. Create an export directory and copy protobuf message logs (*.pb)</h1>
<p dir="auto">mkdir -p ~/antigravity-export<br>
cp ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/implicit/*.pb ~/antigravity-export/</p>
<h1 dir="auto">3. Copy conversation indexes and plain text logs</h1>
<p dir="auto">cp ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/cache/last_conversations.json ~/antigravity-export/<br>
cp ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/cache/conversation_metadata.json ~/antigravity-export/<br>
cp ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/log/cli-*.log ~/antigravity-export/</p>
<h1 dir="auto">Note:</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">- .db files are standard SQLite and can be read with any SQLite client.</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">- .pb files are protobuf-serialized chat transcripts and require a deserializer to render cleanly.</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">- Media attachments are stored per-conversation in ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain//</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">- State snapshots are in ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/jetski_state.pbtxt</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">Here are the instructions for recuperating the data from Gemini CLI to Antigravity:</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">Option A: Native Import (Recommended)</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">Run the native migration tool directly within Antigravity CLI:</h1>
<p dir="auto">agy plugin import gemini</p>
<h1 dir="auto">Option B: Manual Directory and Transcript Restoration</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">1. Locate the legacy conversation UUID or file you wish to recover from your backup or export folder.</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">2. Create the target structure in Antigravity CLI's brain directory:</h1>
<p dir="auto">TARGET_UUID="your_conversation_uuid_here"<br>
mkdir -p ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/${TARGET_UUID}/.system_generated/logs/<br>
mkdir -p ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/${TARGET_UUID}/scratch/</p>
<h1 dir="auto">3. Copy or Move the transcript JSONL or Protobuf file into the target directory:</h1>
<p dir="auto">cp ~/antigravity-export/${TARGET_UUID}.pb ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/implicit/</p>
<h1 dir="auto">OR if restoring raw transcripts:</h1>
<p dir="auto">cp ~/antigravity-export/transcript.jsonl ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/${TARGET_UUID}/.system_generated/logs/</p>
<h1 dir="auto">4. Refresh and Index the restored session inside Antigravity CLI:</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">Launch agy in your terminal, then run the switch command:</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">/resume or /switch</h1>
<h1 dir="auto">If you don't want to do it manually, pro tip: ask agy (antigravity). I'm pretty sure agy can do this with its eyes closed, and it'll charge you about $60 in tool costs from all the agents, subagents, and helpers it spawns. It'll have absolutely no problem ingesting your entire /home directory and the past 10 years of unrelated activity just to "achieve full context". But by God, it will export the shit out of your conversations. It'll do exactly what you asked for, and it will bankrupt you in the process if you're on an API tier. If you're lucky enough to be on a Pro plan, it'll wipe out your entire weekly allowance PLUS the five hour quota, and if you're lucky, it'll locate, export, and ingest your data BEFORE the 5 hour limit and the whole week of quota runs out. Your call. You can do it manually, or you can risk it. :)</h1>
<h1 dir="auto"></h1>
<h1 dir="auto">Hope that helps :)</h1>
    </td>
